1.note: The author is speaking as if the leaders of the tribes of Israel were the **heads** of those tribes. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the leaders of the tribes]

2.q: אִישׁ֩ כִּֽי יִדֹּ֨ר נֶ֜דֶר לַֽ⁠יהוָ֗ה אֽוֹ הִשָּׁ֤בַע שְׁבֻעָה֙ לֶ⁠אְסֹ֤ר אִסָּר֙ עַל נַפְשׁ֔⁠וֹ לֹ֥א יַחֵ֖ל דְּבָר֑⁠וֹ
2.note: Moses is presenting a possible condition, that a man might make a vow or swear an oath to Yahweh. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. It may also be helpful to reorder this sentence so that the conditional statement comes first. Alternate translation: [If a man vows a vow to Yahweh or swears an oath to bind a bond on his life, he shall not profane his word]

Here and throughout the chapter, the word **bond** could mean: (1) that the person has formally committed to an agreement with someone. Alternate translation: [to commit to a binding contract] (2) that the person has made a promise to abstain from something. Alternate translation: [to refrain from doing something]

Moses is not referring to a specific **man**. He means men in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Any man]

2.q: יִדֹּ֨ר נֶ֜דֶר לַֽ⁠יהוָ֗ה אֽוֹ הִשָּׁ֤בַע שְׁבֻעָה֙ לֶ⁠אְסֹ֤ר אִסָּר֙ עַל נַפְשׁ֔⁠וֹ
2.note: Moses is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this.

Moses is using **to bind a bond on his life** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to place himself under a binding obligation.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to place himself under a binding obligation]

Moses is using **he shall not profane his word** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he must not break his promise.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he must not break his promise]

Here, **going out from his mouth** represents what the man has said. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [According to everything that he has spoken]

3.note: Moses is not referring to a specific **woman**. He means women in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And any woman]

The implication is that this woman is young and unmarried and so is still living under the authority of her father. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the house of her father while she is still young and unmarried]

4.note: Moses is using **keeps silent to her** as a common expression of the culture to mean “says nothing to oppose what she has done.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and her father says nothing to oppose what she has done]

Moses is using **shall stand** as a common expression of the culture to mean “will remain in force.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [then all her vows shall remain in force]

5.note: Moses is using **on the day of his hearing** as a common expression of the culture to mean “at the time when he learns about it.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when he hears about it]

The implication is that Yahweh will forgive her for not doing what she vowed to do. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh will forgive her for not doing what she vowed to do]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because her father forbade her]

6.note: Moses is repeating forms of the verb **being** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [And if she indeed becomes the wife of a man]

Moses is using **she is for a man** as a common expression of the culture to mean “she becomes the wife of a man.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [she becomes the wife of a man]

Here, **her lips** represent what she has said. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [her thoughtless spoken words]

8.q: וְ֠⁠אִם בְּ⁠י֨וֹם שְׁמֹ֣עַ אִישָׁ⁠הּ֮ יָנִ֣יא אוֹתָ⁠הּ֒
8.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about her husband forbidding her before the information about the day when he hears about her vow. Alternate translation: [And if her husband forbids her on the day of his hearing]

Moses is using **breaks her vow** as a common expression of the culture to mean “cancels her vow.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [then he cancels her vow]

9.note: The expression **driven out** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and one whom her husband has sent away]

Moses is using **one driven out** as a common expression of the culture to mean “a woman whose husband has divorced her.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and a divorced woman]

The implication is that no one else has the authority to cancel what such a woman has promised. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [shall stand upon her, since no one has the authority to cancel it]

10.note: Here, Moses could be speaking about: (1) a new situation, that of a woman who is married when she makes the vow or agreement. This situation is the topic of 30:10–15. Alternate translation: [And as for a married woman, if in the house of her husband she vowed] (2) the same situation, that of a widowed or divorced woman. In this case, Moses is explaining what the instructions are for vows and agreements she made before her husband died or divorced her. This situation is the topic of 30:10–12 or 30:10–15, and the tense of the verbs in those verses should be changed to the far past. Alternate translation: [And if she had previously vowed in the house of her husband before he died or divorced her]

11.note: The terms **keeps silent to her** and **does not forbid her** mean similar things. Moses is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [and he says nothing at all to oppose her]

12.note: Moses is repeating forms of the verb **breaks** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [And if her husband completely cancels them]

12.q: כָּל מוֹצָ֨א שְׂפָתֶ֧י⁠הָ לִ⁠נְדָרֶ֛י⁠הָ וּ⁠לְ⁠אִסַּ֥ר נַפְשָׁ֖⁠הּ לֹ֣א יָק֑וּם אִישָׁ֣⁠הּ הֲפֵרָ֔⁠ם
12.note: Moses does not use a connecting word here, but the second sentence gives the reason for the result that the first sentence describes. If it would be more natural in your language, you could state the reason first and use a connector such as “because.” Alternate translation: [because her husband has broken them, all that goes out of her lips for her vows and for the bond of her life shall not stand]

13.q: כָּל נֵ֛דֶר וְ⁠כָל שְׁבֻעַ֥ת אִסָּ֖ר לְ⁠עַנֹּ֣ת נָ֑פֶשׁ אִישָׁ֥⁠הּ יְקִימֶ֖⁠נּוּ
13.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about what her husband may do before the information about the vows and oaths that he may act on. Alternate translation: [Her husband may make stand every vow and every oath of a bond to humble a soul]

Moses is using the possessive form to describe an **oath** that is characterized by a **bond**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a binding oath]

Moses is using **to humble a soul** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to deny oneself something, such as by going without food.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to deny oneself something]

14.note: Moses is repeating forms of the verb **keeps silent** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [And if her husband remains completely silent toward her]

Moses is using **from day to day** as a common expression of the culture to mean “as one day follows another.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as one day follows another]

Moses is using **makes stand** as a common expression of the culture to mean “confirms that they remain in force.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [then he confirms all her vows]

15.note: Moses is using **he shall lift up her iniquity** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he will bear the guilt for what she did not do.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [then he shall bear the guilt for what she did not do]

16.q: בֵּ֥ין אִ֖ישׁ לְ⁠אִשְׁתּ֑⁠וֹ בֵּֽין אָ֣ב לְ⁠בִתּ֔⁠וֹ
16.note: Moses is using **between a man to his wife, between a father to his daughter** as a common expression of the culture to mean “concerning the relationship of a man to his wife and of a father to his daughter.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [concerning the relationship of a man to his wife and of a father to his daughter]
